# Book I, Proposition 8

*Two sides and the base make the angles equal*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have also the base equal to the base, they will also have the angles equal which are contained by the equal straight lines.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved, as Euclid states it · Euclid's argument

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/08-idea.svg" alt="If all three sides match (red, blue and black), the angle between the red and blue sides matches too (yellow), however the triangle is turned." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>If all three sides match (red, blue and black), the angle between the red and blue sides matches too (yellow), however the triangle is turned.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/08.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.8, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let ABC, DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF respectively, namely AB to DE, and AC to DF; and let them have the base BC equal to the base EF;

I say that the angle BAC is also equal to the angle EDF.

For, if the triangle ABC be applied to the triangle DEF, and if the point B be placed on the point E and the straight line BC on EF,

the point C will also coincide with F,

because BC is equal to EF.

Then, BC coinciding with EF,

BA, AC will also coincide with ED, DF;

for, if the base BC coincides with the base EF, and the sides BA, AC do not coincide with ED, DF but fall beside them as EG, GF,

then, given two straight lines constructed on a straight line (from its extremities) and meeting in a point, there will have been constructed on the same straight line (from its extremities), and on the same side of it, two other straight lines meeting in another point and equal to the former two respectively, namely each to that which has the same extremity with it.

But they cannot be so constructed. [I. 7]

Therefore it is not possible that, if the base BC be applied to the base EF, the sides BA, AC should not coincide with ED, DF;

they will therefore coincide,

so that the angle BAC will also coincide with the angle EDF, and will be equal to it.

If therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop08.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop08.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out. The list below marks where several sentences share one step; the `/- … -/` notes in the listing explain smaller adjustments.

**How the Lean follows the text**

- **Carried together.** "for, if the base BC coincides with the base EF…" Our I.7 is stated positively, so Euclid's reduction to the impossible is one step: I.7 shows that G, where A comes down, is D itself.

```lean
/-- If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have also the base
equal to the base, they will also have the angles equal which are contained by the equal
straight lines. -/
theorem Prop8 {A B C D E F : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hDEF : Triangle D E F)
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖D E‖) (hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖D F‖) (hBC : ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖) :
    ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F := by
  -- Let ABC, DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF
  -- respectively, namely AB to DE, and AC to DF; and let them have the base BC equal to the
  -- base EF;
  -- I say that the angle BAC is also equal to the angle EDF.
  -- For, if the triangle ABC be applied to the triangle DEF, and if the point B be placed on
  -- the point E and the straight line BC on EF,
  /- To lay BC along EF we need the straight line EF itself (Postulate 1). The
     rule of superposition then sets B on E, sends C along the ray from E through
     F, and lets us choose the side of EF on which A comes down: D's side, so
     that the two triangles lie over one another, as Euclid's word "applied"
     means. The copy of ABC is `G E C'`: C lands at C' and A at G. -/
  have hEF : E ≠ F := hDEF.ne₂₃
  obtain ⟨EF, hE_EF, hF_EF⟩ := Postulate1 E F hEF
  have hD_EF : ¬ OnLine D EF := fun hD => hDEF ⟨EF, hD, hE_EF, hF_EF⟩
  obtain ⟨C', G, hC'_EF, hC'_ray, hGD_EF, hEC', hC'G, hGE, -, hEGC', -⟩ :=
    superposition hABC.bca hE_EF hF_EF hEF hD_EF
  -- the point C will also coincide with F,
  -- because BC is equal to EF.
  /- C lands on the ray from E through F, as far from E as F is; on a ray only one
     point is at that distance (`OnRay.eq_of_len_eq` in Book Zero). -/
  have hEC'_EF : ‖E C'‖ = ‖E F‖ := hEC'.trans hBC
  have hC'F : C' = F :=
    OnRay.eq_of_len_eq ⟨hEF, (ne_of_len_eq hEC'_EF hEF).symm, ⟨EF, hE_EF, hF_EF, hC'_EF⟩, hC'_ray⟩
      hEC'_EF
  -- Then, BC coinciding with EF,
  -- BA, AC will also coincide with ED, DF;
  /- The sides BA, AC have been carried to GE, GF, and they are equal to ED, DF. -/
  have hGE_DE : ‖G E‖ = ‖D E‖ := hGE.trans hAB
  have hGF_DF : ‖G F‖ = ‖D F‖ :=
    calc ‖G F‖ = ‖F G‖ := len_symm G F
      _ = ‖C' G‖ := by rw [hC'F]
      _ = ‖C A‖ := hC'G
      _ = ‖A C‖ := len_symm C A
      _ = ‖D F‖ := hAC
  -- for, if the base BC coincides with the base EF, and the sides BA, AC do not coincide with
  -- ED, DF but fall beside them as EG, GF,
  -- then, given two straight lines constructed on a straight line (from its extremities) and
  -- meeting in a point, there will have been constructed on the same straight line (from its
  -- extremities), and on the same side of it, two other straight lines meeting in another
  -- point and equal to the former two respectively, namely each to that which has the same
  -- extremity with it.
  /- G and D are on the same side of EF: superposition put G there. And since
     two points fix one straight line, that is the same side of "the straight
     line EF" however it is named (`SameSideOf.of_line` in Book Zero). -/
  have hGD_side : SameSideOf G D E F := SameSideOf.of_line hEF hE_EF hF_EF hGD_EF
  -- But they cannot be so constructed. [I. 7]
  -- Therefore it is not possible that, if the base BC be applied to the base EF, the sides BA,
  -- AC should not coincide with ED, DF;
  -- they will therefore coincide,
  /- Our I.7 is stated positively: two such points are one and the same point.
     So Euclid's reduction to the impossible is a single step here. -/
  have hGD : G = D := Prop7 hGD_side hGE_DE hGF_DF
  -- so that the angle BAC will also coincide with the angle EDF, and will be equal to it.
  /- The angle BAC was carried to the angle EGC', and G is D, C' is F. -/
  have hEGC'_EDF : ∠ E G C' = ∠ E D F := CommonNotion4.angle rfl hGD hC'F
  exact hEGC'.symm.trans hEGC'_EDF
  -- If therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

**Reading the figure**

- [`between_cases`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L74) (through [`OnRay.eq_of_len_eq`](../../Elements/Figure/Rays.lean#L159)): Of three different points on a straight line, one is between the other two. (Between 6)
- [`between_of_between_left`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L66): If B is between A and C, and D is between A and B, then D is between A and C. (Between 4)
- [`between_of_between_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L70): If B is between A and C, and C is between B and D, then B is between A and D. (Between 5)
- [`between_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L43): If B is between A and C, it is between C and A. (Between 1)
- [`centre_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L35): The centre of a circle is inside it. (Generalities 3)
- [`circles_meet`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L201): If each circle passes through a point inside the other, the circles cut one another. This is the step Euclid takes for granted in I.1. (Intersection 5)
- [`circles_meet_same_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L81): Two circles that cut one another do so on each side of the straight line through their centres. (Intersections 8)
- [`exists_point`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L26) (through [`Triangle.ne₂₃`](../../Elements/Figure/Triangles.lean#L29)): Let a point be taken. (Points 1)
- [`exists_point_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L38): Let a point be taken between B and C. (Points 3)
- [`line_circle_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L69): A straight line through a point B inside a circle, heading out to a point C outside it, cuts the circle between B and C. (Intersections 4)
- [`line_circle_beyond`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L75): A straight line through a point B inside a circle, produced beyond B away from C, cuts the circle there. (Intersections 5)
- [`line_unique`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L28) (through [`SameSideOf.of_line`](../../Elements/Figure/Sides.lean#L32)): Two points determine a straight line. (Generalities 1)
- [`lines_meet_of_opposite_sides`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L179): A straight line joining points on opposite sides of L crosses L. (Intersection 1)
- [`ne_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L46): A point between two others differs from the first. (Between 1)
- [`ne_of_between_ends`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L49): The ends of a finite straight line differ. (Between 1)
- [`not_between_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L52): If B is between A and C, then A is not between B and C. (Between 1)
- [`not_between_of_between_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L79): If B is between A and C, and also between A and D, then B is not between C and D: C and D lie on the same side of B. (Between 7)
- [`not_on_line_of_same_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L92): Points on one side of a straight line are not on it. (Same side 3)
- [`on_line_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L56): A straight line through A and B, with B between A and C, passes through C. (Between 2)
- [`on_line_of_between_ends`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L61): A straight line through A and C passes through every point between them. (Between 3)
- [`pasch2`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L111): If B is between A and C, A is on L and B is off it, then B and C are on the same side of L: a straight line that leaves L at A does not cross it again. (Pasch 2)
- [`pasch3`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L114): A straight line through a point between A and C separates them. (Pasch 3)
- [`pasch4`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L119): If two different straight lines L and M meet at B, and A and C are points of M, different from each other and from B, that are not on the same side of L, then B is between A and C. (Pasch 4)
- [`same_side_or`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L99): A straight line has only two sides. (Same side 5)
- [`same_side_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L89): If A is on the same side of a straight line as B, then B is on the same side as A. (Same side 2)
- [`same_side_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L96): Two points on the same side of a straight line as a third point are on the same side as each other. (Same side 4)
- [`triple_incidence1`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L131): Take B on L, C on M and D on N, three straight lines through A. If C lies within the angle BAD (on D's side of L and on B's side of N), then B and D are not on the same side of M: the straight line AC separates them. (Triple incidence 1)
- [`triple_incidence2`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L139): Take B on L, C on M and D on N, three straight lines through A, with B other than A and D off M. If C and D are on the same side of L, and B and D are not on the same side of M, then B and C are on the same side of N: C lies within the angle BAD. (Triple incidence 2)

**Lengths, angles and areas**

- [`angle_add_of_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L54): If D lies within the angle BAC, then BAC is made up of BAD and DAC. (Diagram-angle 2)

- [`len_lt_of_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L37): A point inside is nearer the centre than the circumference. (Diagram-segment 4)

- [`len_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L23) (used here): The straight line AB is the straight line BA. (Metric 3)
- [`same_ray_of_angle_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L49): If the angle BAC is nothing, C lies on the ray from A through B. (Diagram-angle 1)

**Superposition**

- [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean#L30) (used here): **Superposition.** The triangle ABC can be applied to the straight line L with A on D, B on the ray from D through G, and C on the side of L where H is, without changing any side or angle.

**Laws of magnitude**

- [`add_comm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L26): The order of adding does not matter. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L45): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)
- [`add_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L29): Adding nothing changes nothing. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_irrefl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L32) (through [`OnRay.eq_of_len_eq`](../../Elements/Figure/Rays.lean#L159)): No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L35): What is less than the less is less still. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L39) (through [`OnRay.eq_of_len_eq`](../../Elements/Figure/Rays.lean#L159)): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. (System E §3.5)
- [`not_lt_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L42) (through [`OnRay.eq_of_len_eq`](../../Elements/Figure/Rays.lean#L159)): Nothing is less than zero. (System E §3.5)

## Mishnah

_Our commentary: what Euclid assumes, what Lean made us say out loud, and how the result looks by modern means._

Heath calls I.8 "a *partial* converse of I. 4" (vol. 1, p. 262): the equal bases, which I.4 proves, are given here, and the angle is proved instead. Euclid goes no further than the angles at the vertices A and D, because, as Heath explains after Proclus and Henry Savile, "when once the vertical angles are proved equal, the rest follows from I. 4, and there is no object in proving again what has been proved already" (vol. 1, p. 262).

For the second time Euclid picks up a triangle and lays it on another. Our rule [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean) returns newly placed points: a copy of ABC with B on E, C on the ray from E through F, and A on the chosen side of EF. We permit its direct use only in I.4 and I.8. That policy limits its use; as a construction principle it is stronger than System E's restricted inference rule. Euclid never says which side A comes down on, but I.7 needs to know, since D and its mirror image in EF are each as far from E and from F as the other; so we ask for D's side, which is what "applied" means. C lands on F "because BC is equal to EF", and because BC was laid along EF, as in I.4. Then Euclid's reduction to the impossible, in which BA, AC "fall beside" ED, DF, becomes one citation of `Prop7`: G, where A comes down, is D. The Greek verb, Heath notes, means "to pass by without touching," "to miss" or "to deviate" (vol. 1, p. 262).

I.8 may once have said more. Aristotle, speaking of the rainbow, concludes that "*the triangles are equal*", and J. L. Heiberg took this for a trace of an older I.8: "we see here therefore, in a clear example, how the stones of the ancient fabric were recut for the rigid structure of his *Elements*" (Heath, vol. 1, pp. 262–263). Heath doubts the inference is safe. Proclus also preserves a proof by Philo that lays ABC on the far side of EF and uses I.5 in place of I.7, and Heath finds that "it is elegant; but it is inconvenient in one respect, since three cases have to be distinguished" (vol. 1, p. 263). David Hilbert, who made side, angle, side an axiom, proves side, side, side from it with no moving of figures.

## Further reading

- David Hilbert's [*The Foundations of Geometry*](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/17384) (1902, free online), in E. J. Townsend's translation, is the short, surprisingly readable book that writes down the axioms Euclid took for granted; ch. I, "The Five Groups of Axioms", makes side, angle, side one of them.
- To see superposition as a motion of the plane, read Felix Klein's Erlangen Programme of 1872, ["A comparative review of recent researches in geometry"](https://arxiv.org/abs/0807.3161) (1893, free online), in M. W. Haskell's translation: the short manifesto behind the idea that a geometry is defined by the motions it allows.
